audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 1 Kings / Melakhim Aleph chapter 10, first-pass draft aligned to public-domain verse structure; formal witness and trade-history audit remains required.
audit_status.review_note: Reviewed for the queen of Sheba's agency, intellectual exchange, court labor, royal spectacle, diplomatic gifts, exoticized trade, gold concentration, ivory, animals, militarization, Egyptian horse trade, and wisdom-versus-extraction tension.

verses.restored: Queen of Sheba heard report of Solomon concerning name of YHWH, and she came to test him with difficult questions.
She came to Jerusalem with a very great company, camels carrying spices, very much gold, and precious stones. She came to Solomon and spoke with him all that was upon her heart.
Solomon answered all her matters; no matter was hidden from king that he could not explain to her.
Queen of Sheba saw all wisdom of Solomon and house he built,
food of his table, seating of servants, attendance of ministers, their garments, cupbearers, and his ascent/burnt offering by which he went to house of YHWH; there was no more breath in her.
She said to king, True was word I heard in my land concerning your words/deeds and wisdom.
I did not believe words until I came and my eyes saw. Look, half was not told me; your wisdom and prosperity exceed report I heard.
Happy are your people/men; happy are these your servants who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom.
Blessed be YHWH your Divine, who delighted in you to place you upon throne of Israel. Because YHWH loved Israel forever, YHWH made you king to do justice and righteousness.
She gave king one hundred twenty talents of gold, very great abundance of spices, and precious stones. Never again came such abundance of spices as Queen of Sheba gave King Solomon.
Hiram's fleet that brought gold from Ophir also brought from Ophir very great amounts of almug wood and precious stones.
King made from almug wood supports for house of YHWH and king's house, and lyres and harps for singers. Such almug wood had not come or been seen until this day.
King Solomon gave Queen of Sheba all her desire, whatever she asked, besides what he gave her according to royal hand. She turned and went to her land, she and her servants.
Weight of gold coming to Solomon in one year was six hundred sixty-six talents of gold,
besides from traders, merchant traffic, all kings of Arabia, and governors of land.
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of hammered gold; six hundred shekels of gold went upon each shield.
He made three hundred small shields of hammered gold; three minas of gold went upon each shield. King placed them in House of Forest of Lebanon.
The king made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with refined gold.
The throne had six steps, a rounded top behind, arms on both sides of seat, and two lions standing beside arms.
Twelve lions stood there upon six steps, one on each side. Nothing like it was made for any kingdom.
All King Solomon's drinking vessels were gold, and all vessels of House of Forest of Lebanon were pure gold; silver was considered as nothing in days of Solomon.
King had a fleet of Tarshish at sea with Hiram's fleet. Once in three years fleet came bearing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks/baboons.
King Solomon became greater than all kings of earth in riches and wisdom.
All earth sought face of Solomon to hear wisdom Divine had put in his heart.
Each brought gift: vessels of silver and gold, garments, weapons, spices, horses, and mules, a yearly amount.
Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen. He had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, stationed in chariot cities and with king in Jerusalem.
King made silver in Jerusalem like stones, and cedars like sycamores in lowland for abundance.
Solomon's horses were imported from Egypt and Kue; king's merchants acquired them from Kue at a price.
A chariot came up and went out from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse for one hundred fifty. Thus through their hand they exported them to all kings of Hittites and kings of Aram.

translation_notes: The queen of Sheba is a sovereign intellectual and diplomatic actor who travels with resources, questions Solomon, evaluates his court, blesses YHWH, negotiates exchange, and returns to her own country.
Her astonishment includes servants, ministers, food, dress, architecture, and ritual. Court magnificence depends upon extensive labor and disciplined hierarchy.
Her blessing names justice and righteousness as the purpose of kingship; wealth and reputation are not the standard.
Spices, gold, gems, rare wood, ivory, animals, horses, and textiles come through long-distance networks involving extraction, animal capture, transport danger, and workers absent from the narrative.
The ivory throne requires killed elephants or traded tusks; animal bodies are part of royal spectacle.
Gold shields and vessels convert extreme wealth into display while silver loses value at court. Abundance concentrated at the center does not prove equitable prosperity.
Apes and other animals brought as exotic cargo should not be romanticized; capture and transport likely involved suffering.
Chariot and horse accumulation conflicts with Torah's warnings about royal militarization and return to Egypt.
The chapter intentionally moves from a woman praising justice to an inventory of excess, inviting the reader to test Solomon's wisdom against his accumulation.
safety_note: Do not exoticize the queen of Sheba, erase her sovereignty, or reduce her to admiration of a male king. Do not present ivory, captured animals, gold concentration, tribute, or arms trading as uncomplicated blessing. Measure wisdom by justice and righteousness.
